prospect of whitby.fact: Riverside Wapping pub usually dated to 1520; a strong fit for the heritage-by-water demo.
The Prospect of Whitby is a Grade II* listed pub on Wapping Wall in the East End, reputed to be one of the oldest riverside taverns in London, dating from around 1520.

the grapes.fact: Limehouse pub on Narrow Street with a long river-facing history and a visible place in Hilton's pub print shop.
The Grapes is a Grade II listed public house at 76 Narrow Street, Limehouse, on the north bank of the Thames; a pub has stood on the site since 1583.

the dove.fact: Upper Mall riverside pub in Hammersmith; useful as a west London water-side heritage stop.
The Dove is a Grade II* listed pub on Upper Mall, Hammersmith, overlooking the Thames; it holds a Guinness World Record for the smallest bar room in a public house.

the old pack horse.fact: Chiswick High Road pub noted for its Edwardian exterior and strong local character.
The Old Pack Horse is a Grade II listed pub on Chiswick High Road, rebuilt in 1910 in an Edwardian style for the Isleworth Brewery.

the lamb.fact: Victorian Bloomsbury pub with the kind of preserved interior detail that suits a heritage crawl.
The Lamb is a Grade II listed public house on Lamb's Conduit Street, Bloomsbury, noted for its surviving Victorian snob screens above the bar.

the sun tavern.fact: Bethnal Green pub included in Hilton's visible pub print shop, useful for a writer-inspired crawl seed.
On the writer's print trail as one of Alastair Hilton's photographed London pubs.

the queens head.fact: One of the app's closest matches for Hilton's visible The Queens print; kept as a soft match until the exact pub is verified.
A candidate stop on the writer's Queens print trail, pending confirmation of the exact venue.

the queens arms.fact: Pimlico pub from 1846; a useful Victorian reference stop for the seeded heritage route.
A Victorian-era Pimlico pub kept as a reference stop for the heritage crawl.

the nellie dean.fact: The Nellie Dean of Soho is a Grade II listed pub at 89 Dean Street, Soho; the present building dates from 1900 and there has been a pub on the site since the 18th century.

the dog & duck.fact: The Dog and Duck at 18 Bateman Street, Soho, is a Grade II listed pub; the current building dates from 1897 and its upstairs dining room is named after the writer George Orwell, who was a regular.

the coach & horses.fact: The Coach and Horses at 29 Greek Street, Soho, is a Grade II listed pub long associated with Private Eye magazine and with journalist Jeffrey Bernard, whose 'Low Life' column and the play 'Jeffrey Bernard Is Unwell' immortalised it.

the crown & two chairmen.fact: The Crown & Two Chairmen at 31-32 Dean Street, Soho, has had a pub on the site since 1736; the present building was rebuilt in 1929 and the name is said to recall two sedan-chair men who drank here while Queen Anne sat for a portrait opposite.

the coal hole.fact: The Coal Hole is a Grade II listed pub at 91 Strand, part of the Savoy Court development, built in 1903-04 to the design of architect T. E. Collcutt.

the lyceum tavern.fact: The Lyceum Tavern at 354 Strand takes its name from the neighbouring Lyceum Theatre; a tavern has stood on the site since the 1840s and the present building dates from 1906. It is a Grade II listed pub.

the seven stars.fact: The Seven Stars is a Grade II listed pub at 53 Carey Street behind the Royal Courts of Justice; with 17th-century origins (its frontage bears the date 1602), it is one of the few City-fringe pubs to have survived the Great Fire of London.

ye olde cock tavern.fact: Ye Olde Cock Tavern is a Grade II listed pub at 22 Fleet Street, listed in 1977; the tavern was moved across the street and rebuilt in the 1880s, and is traditionally said to have been frequented by Samuel Pepys, Charles Dickens and Alfred Tennyson.

the old bank of england.fact: The Old Bank of England is a Grade II listed pub at 194 Fleet Street, built in 1886 by Sir Arthur Blomfield; it housed the Law Courts branch of the Bank of England from 1888 to 1975 before becoming a pub in 1994.

the tipperary.fact: The Tipperary is a Grade II listed pub at 66 Fleet Street; the building was built in about 1667, and the wood-panelled pub is widely reputed to be one of London's oldest Irish pubs.

museum tavern.fact: The Museum Tavern is a Grade II listed pub at 49 Great Russell Street, opposite the British Museum; the present building was rebuilt around 1855-64 by William Finch Hill, and Karl Marx is traditionally said to have drunk here while working in the nearby Reading Room.

the perseverance.fact: The Perseverance at 63 Lamb's Conduit Street, Bloomsbury, is a Grade II listed building of early-18th-century origin, refronted in the early 19th century; it traded for years as The Sun before taking its current name.

the rugby tavern.fact: The Rugby Tavern on the corner of Great James Street and Rugby Street, Bloomsbury, is a Grade II listed pub dating from about 1850, built on land that forms part of the Rugby (School) Estate.

the dolphin tavern.fact: The Dolphin Tavern at 44 Red Lion Street, Holborn, was badly damaged by a Zeppelin raid on 8 September 1915; the pub's clock, recovered from the rubble, is preserved stopped at 10.40pm, the moment of the blast.

the dickens inn.fact: The Dickens Inn at St Katharine Docks occupies an 18th-century timber-framed former warehouse; when the docks were redeveloped in the 1970s the structure was moved bodily to its present site and reopened as a three-storey balconied inn.

the captain kidd.fact: The Captain Kidd at 108 Wapping High Street is a Grade II listed riverside pub in a converted former warehouse, named after the pirate William Kidd, who was hanged at the nearby Execution Dock in 1701.
